The growing interest in machine learning and data science over the past decade can be attributed to the widespread adoption of cloud-based services, mobile devices, and various digital platforms. As the amount of available data continues to expand, developing systems that can efficiently extract and utilize this knowledge is a pressing concern. Historically, machine learning has been applied in data analysis, such as identifying trends, categorizing data, and making predictions, but recent advancements have led to the development of systems capable of continuous learning, processing new data in real-time and refining their understanding accordingly. This paper will delve into the key features of lifelong learning systems, explore their underlying architecture, and examine potential challenges and research avenues in this field.

One of the key challenges in developing photonic quantum computing lies in manipulating qubits across different degrees of freedom, such as wavelength, direction, and time. Researchers have proposed various techniques, but there has been a lack of universal methods that can transform photonic signals between these degrees of freedom. In this study, we present a novel approach to on-chip coherent transformation of photonic signals between the wavelength and time domains. By utilizing a dual-coupled resonator waveguide, we demonstrate that time-domain signals can be converted into wavelength-domain signals, and vice versa. Furthermore, our findings suggest that this conversion process preserves the quantum correlations of entangled photon pairs. Importantly, the transformation can be controlled by adjusting the cavity parameters, enabling the generation of a wide range of photonic states, including superpositions of any two or more wavelength and time values. This work provides a significant step towards the development of a universal on-chip quantum photonic platform.

We investigated the impact of various types of base pair misalignments on the conduction properties of DNA. Our calculations, performed using the transfer matrix method, analyzed the electronic properties of two parallel DNA strands under different gas environments, focusing on how these irregularities affect the material's bandgap, transmission level, and current flow. The results indicate that base pair misalignments can lead to a significant decrease in the current passing through the DNA, even to the point of complete current blockage. We found that this decrease in current is most pronounced in the off-resonance scenario and occurs when the misalignment distance is greater than the energy difference between the Fermi level and the material's bandgap.

A novel approach for registering multiple 3D point sets is presented, which integrates a clustering technique to reduce the complexity of point set matching. Prior to registration, the approach groups multiple point sets into a limited number of clusters, ensuring each cluster contains a significant number of points to guarantee robust registration. Subsequently, the approach iteratively registers the clusters, which enables the system to adapt to the failure of any node (cluster pair) by recalculating the mean positions of the remaining clusters and updating the clusters. The experimental results validate the robustness, resilience, and efficiency of the proposed approach, especially in the face of node failure, which requires only a minimal number of nodes to fail at any given time.

Our research examined the magnetic structure of Tb3RuO7 using muon spin relaxation and zero-field specific heat measurements.  Our findings indicate that the Tb3RuO7 compound has a non-uniform Ru spin-3/4 chain with alternating Ru-Ru bond interactions, which is influenced by non-uniform magnetic fields generated by the rare-earth Tb3+ ions.  As a result, the compound exhibits a spin-3/2 Ru chain system with an irregular "run-and-tread" arrangement.  This specific arrangement leads to the emergence of a disordered magnetic state characterized by a finite heat capacity at zero temperature and a broad maximum in the temperature dependence of the muon spin-relaxation rate at low temperatures.  These specific heat and muon spin-relaxation measurements are indicative of significant spin fluctuations in the compound at low temperatures.

This study aims to demonstrate the critical role of optimality criteria in resolving DC limited optimization problems. A broad scenario is examined, encompassing various mathematical optimization techniques, including linear, nonlinear, and constrained approaches. A novel approach is developed to tackle unconstrained problems by formulating them as two-way communication systems. Moreover, this method is adapted to address constrained problems, utilizing penalized and relaxed methods. A comprehensive analysis is presented, covering the algorithm's convergence and iteration performance.

We investigate the boundary behavior of the D-brane-induced supergravity solution in AdS$_3\times$S$^3$ for a D$(-1$/D$7$) system. Our findings suggest that the open string partition function for this system does not exhibit a small-distance expansion in the transverse spatial direction, instead suggesting a non-compact boundary geometry. This discrepancy potentially stems from the fact that the metric component describing the compact sphere does not vanish at the boundary, thereby influencing the black hole entropy in the dual holographic CFT$_2$. Furthermore, the small-distance expansion in the transverse spatial direction is likely to be absent due to the presence of this sphere near the boundary. Our analysis also reveals that the asymptotic dilaton does not exhibit a standard behavior, instead tending towards a constant at the boundary, and this constant is likely to be inversely proportional to the level of the CFT$_2$.

The concept of Domain Clashes serves as a diagnostic tool to pinpoint issues arising from the interaction between domain knowledge and the representation capabilities of Machine Learning models. We apply this idea to explain-style transfer from source to target texts, where a source text conveys formal scientific information and is represented by a BiLSTM encoder-decoder. We argue that the decoder's output space should be constrained to align with the semantic and grammatical demands of the target text, in order to prevent the model from exhibiting problematic behavior in response to input domain changes. We illustrate this phenomenon with an example drawn from the Science Questions dataset, where a biassed language model incorrectly answers a question due to an unaddressed conflict between the question's and answer's domains. We propose that the underlying issue is a mismatch between the model's internal representation and the types of questions present in the training data, leading us to term this issue Domain Clashes.

Deep reinforcement learning has successfully demonstrated the capabilities 
of robots in a general-purpose setting, but their practical application in 
real-world environments is hindered by the issue of high sample complexity 
and the risk of failed controllers due to unexpected scenarios. To address 
these problems, we explore the use of control priors in robotic systems. By 
combining a Bayesian approach with prior knowledge of a system's dynamics 
and control strategies, we can significantly reduce the required number of 
training samples. Our proposed method integrates a Bayesian controller with 
a deep reinforcement learning algorithm, resulting in a successful application 
to a real-world robotic scenario. Our findings show that the incorporation 
of a Bayesian controller and control priors enables robust and efficient 
reinforcement learning for real-world robotic systems.

Perfusion imaging plays a critical role in identifying and quantifying ischemic damage, which can be further analyzed by studying the distribution of contrast agent in the brain. However, this information is often lost in standard deconvolution methods, which smooth out excessive contrast agent accumulation. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes an alternative deconvolution technique, which utilizes a differentiable approach to minimize smoothing and instead mitigate convolved noise. The method was tested using synthetic data and clinical cases related to stroke, and the results showed that it outperforms traditional deconvolution, leading to more precise quantification of perfusion and a lower false-positive rate.

We investigate the theoretical aspects of zero-jetness beam operations in collinear perturbative theory by using N$^3$LO QED to determine the electron beam function. This study involves the application of certain properties in the momentum space to identify the structure of the beam at the N$^3$LO level. We further explore the implications of the beam function on the shape of the differential cross section for a specific process, specifically the forward photon yield in $e^+ e^-$ collisions at a luminous factor of 10$^{12}$. The forward photon distribution at the N$^3$LO level is found to exhibit a significant reduction in scale variation for lower values of the photon energy, which leads to a decrease in the forward photon yield. This decrease in the forward photon yield is found to be substantial, specifically around 1.25% at a scale of 0.1 TeV and around 7% at a scale of 0.01 TeV. The forward photon distribution at the N$^3$LO level is found to exhibit a significant reduction in scale variation for lower values of the photon energy, which leads to a decrease in the forward photon yield. This decrease in the forward photon yield is found to be substantial, specifically around 1.25% at a scale of 0.1 TeV and around 7% at a scale of 0.01 TeV.

The power graph of a finite group G, denoted as PG(G), can be visualized by including an edge between each pair of elements from G, provided that one element is a power of the other. In this study, we investigate chordal and path-chained sets within PG(G), and introduce the concept of strongly chordal groups. Notably, we demonstrate that symmetric and alternating groups are strongly chordal. Conversely, we establish that the direct product of A4 and a finite group is not power chordal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that strongly chordal groups have a maximum diameter of 5 within PG(G), and also show that strongly chordal groups are path-chained sets and power chordal. Lastly, we introduce a novel characterization of power chordal sets and power chordal groups.

In target source separation, we attempt to recover the underlying signal of a target sound within a complex mixture of sounds. This paper presents a novel technique called optimal state training for target source separation, which involves creating a model that closely mimics the spectral state of the target sound. By doing so, when we apply the state transition matrix to the current spectral state, we obtain a representation that closely resembles the target sound. Once we have an accurate representation, we can use it as the new spectral state, thereby achieving the optimal outcome. Our approach is unique in that it doesn't require any specific information about the target sound, and it works effectively with any type of sound mixture. As a result, we can use any standard algorithm to directly extract the target sound from the complex mixture. Our experiments show that this method performs better than other techniques and even surpasses the performance of human listeners in certain aspects.

This paper delves into characterizing quantum coherence within the framework of general quantum measurements, which encompass both selective and non-invasive measurements. It is demonstrated that a quantum state is uniquely defined by a set of generalized quantum mutual information terms if and only if the state exhibits coherence relative to the set of generalized quantum observations. Furthermore, we establish that these information-quantum mutual information terms are also sufficient to identify and quantify coherence within the ensemble of Gaussian quantum states. Importantly, we find that these information-quantum mutual information terms offer a promising approach for quantifying coherence in continuous-variable systems, which may lead to new insights and understanding of the phenomenon of coherence.

The type C quasi-periodic oscillations in low mass X-ray binaries are considered to originate from the innermost accretion flow. By analyzing the type C quasi-periodic oscillations in several outbursts of the black hole X-ray binary H 1743--322, we investigated the accretion flow around the black hole. The type C quasi-periodic oscillations in each outburst have distinct characteristics, including their frequencies, amplitudes, and outburst phases. By correlating these features with the accretion flow, we determined the radius of the type C quasi-periodic oscillations in each outburst. The results suggest that the innermost accretion flow around the black hole was highly compressed and eventually formed a thin disk during the outburst. The accretion flow structure in each outburst is consistent with a model of a thin disk surrounded by a hot corona. The type C quasi-periodic oscillations in each outburst are likely triggered by a turbulence-driven instability in the thin disk.

In many countries, understanding government policies has become increasingly complicated due to their complexity and the vast amount of information released. This research project aims to address this issue by creating a platform that simplifies understanding through question-and-answer technology. The system is based on a trained neural network model, which is publicly accessible and can be improved upon by a community. The system is intended to be a collaborative platform where users can contribute to its improvement, while also being easily understandable by both government officials and ordinary citizens, regardless of policy complexities.

Recent research conducted by the EAGLE collaboration has provided new insights into the properties of exotic baryon states. Specifically, their study examined the $T_{zz} = 0$ states in the $\bar{d}d$ channel, which are analogous to the well-known $\Lambda(1405)$ particle. The investigation utilized an effective field theory approach, which enabled the calculation of the binding energies and width of the $T_{zz} = 0$ states. The calculated binding energies are consistent with previous findings, indicating that these states are tightly bound by approximately 50 MeV. The results also show that their widths are relatively narrow, with the $T_{zz} = 0^+$ state exhibiting a width of about 50 MeV and the $T_{zz} = 0^-$ state showing a width of around 80 MeV. The study found that the $T_{zz} = 0^+$ state is more stable than the $T_{zz} = 0^-$ state. The calculated binding energies and width of the $T_{zz} = 0$ states are in agreement with experimental data, which further supports the hypothesis that these states are closely related to the $\Lambda(1405)$ particle. The study also explored the properties of the $T_{zz} = 0$ states under different conditions, such as varying baryon mass and coupling constant, which could lead to a deeper understanding of their nature.

Determining the optimal most efficient algorithm for a specific task is referred to as the division problem. A leftmost divider of a set of numbers indicates its ability to be divided by another number. The task of identifying all the leftmost dividers of a set that is less than or equal to a certain value, known as the size constraint k, is a problem in computational number theory. There are two variations of this problem, one where the size of the dividers is minimized and the other where all the possible dividers are identified. Since the 1970s, researchers have been working on these two problems, and by now, an algorithm with a time complexity of O(n log n) has been developed for the first problem, and the second problem can be solved in O(k). Although the two problems are highly related, they are difficult to solve together in a single, efficient algorithm. A new approach presented in this paper is able to find all the leftmost dividers of a set that are less than or above a certain value, and it does so in a time complexity of O(k).

We have conducted a search for transient events in the centers of 29 galaxies that have previously experienced starburst or are currently dormant, using the Hubble Space Telescope to observe them in their UV spectrum. These galaxies were observed over a period of 5-7 years through the HST's HST/COS spectrometer. A total of 11 of the galaxies we studied displayed transient events in their UV spectra, with transient characteristics including variations in brightness, line strength, and line width. A classification of the transients was made based on their properties, with transient types including 3 Terafountains, 2 Terafountains with broad lines, 2 Wolf-Rayet-like AGN, 2 Wolf-Rayet-like transients, 2 Hot Terafountains, 1 Broad-Line Terafountain, 1 Hot AGN, and 1 Wolf-Rayet-like AGN. A comparison of the observed transient characteristics with previously reported data showed a good match. Our findings indicate that transient events in a galaxy's center are a common occurrence, with transient rates possibly exceeding 10% of galaxies that have previously experienced starburst. Our results also suggest that transient events may be a primary mechanism for the creation of supermassive black holes.

In reconfigurable wireless networks, the increasing number of devices and applications create opportunities and challenges. To address this, we focus on developing an advanced scheduler that efficiently manages resources in these networks. We propose a Performer-Critic learning-based scheduler that simultaneously considers application quality requirements and the benefits of switching network configurations. The proposed scheduler consists of two main components: a Critic that estimates the total reward and a Performer that recommends the optimal network configuration. The proposed approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of meeting quality requirements and network configuration switching.

The effectiveness of post-editing tasks heavily relies on the quality of machine-translated texts. While various word-level evaluation metrics are widely used, they have limitations in accurately predicting post-editing difficulties. This study introduces a novel metric that utilizes a neural-based classifier to gauge translation quality at a word level, taking into account multiple factors. The proposed metric's performance was tested on three languages and compared with existing word-level and sentence-level metrics. The results indicate that our word-level metric performs better than the comparisons and accurately reflects the magnitude of post-editing efforts, even in large-scale scenarios.

We investigate how the information about the parameter 'a' in the Kerr-de Sitter spacetime model can be derived from the observed images of black holes. To create these models, we use the supermassive black hole M87* and the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) observations, along with the radio and high-energy observations of the Galactic Center black hole. Our findings indicate that the image of the Kerr-de Sitter black hole is very similar to that of the Schwarzschild model. Therefore, the available EHT data cannot provide distinct information about the parameter 'a'. Furthermore, the image of M87* is very similar to its Schwarzschild counterpart, preventing the use of the observed image for determining 'a'. However, the image of the Galactic Center black hole offers some, albeit limited, information about 'a'. We also discuss the potential of future observations with the next-generation Very Long Baseline Array to improve our understanding of the parameter 'a' through the study of the shadow silhouette of Sgr A*.

The relativistic Einfeldt flux solver, a numerical technique used for astrophysical simulations, is based on an enhanced version of the Lovelace-Parmi approach. This approach, first introduced in a one-dimensional framework, has been adapted for two-dimensional Cartesian coordinates, with a detailed derivation presented in this study. The improved formulation of the RHE achieves a numerical resolution of $O(\Delta x^{\frac{4}{5}} \Delta t)$, which is a significant enhancement over the original Einfeldt flux solver's resolution of $O(\Delta x^{\frac{3}{4}} \Delta t)$. The improved method was tested in a series of numerical simulations, which demonstrated its improved resolution and accuracy. Furthermore, the RHE was found to be insensitive to the specific choice of the function $f(\Delta x/\Delta t)$, which determines the numerical technique's behavior at relativistic speeds; this property was also observed in the Lovelace-Parmi approach.

The LHCb experiment analyzed proton-proton collision data, searching for the mesons $D^{*+}_{s1}$, $D^{*+}_{s2}$, $D^{*+}_{s3}$, $D^{*+}_{s4}$, $D^{*+}_{s5}$, and $D^{*+}_{s6}$ within the $D^{*+} K^0_{\rm S}$ and $D^{*0} K^+$ final states. The data revealed the discovery of $D^{*+}_{s4}$ and $D^{*+}_{s5}$, along with the determination of their masses, decay widths, and branching ratios. The findings are consistent with the assignment of the observed resonances as $D^{*+}_{s3}$ and $D^{*+}_{s4}$, which are the orbitally excited states of $D^{*}_{s}$, based on the one-meson-exchange model.

We investigate fractal polynomials on the Sierpiński gasket with boundaries and express the fractal polynomial functions as linear combinations of scaled fractal functions. We derive integral representations for the polynomials' derivatives on the Sierpiński gasket and show that the fractal polynomial set forms a Banach space. We derive the polynomials' finite-dimensional range for each $k$, and in doing so, find the limit dimension of the range for the polynomials. We also derive the limit dimension of the range for the derivative of the polynomials.

Visual inquiry questions are queries that aim to investigate specific design solutions.  While various types of questions (e.g. what, how, why) can be formulated as visual inquiries, they tend to yield distinct types of design information.  However, current design generation systems struggle to generate such questions based on the desired design outcome, as they are trained to produce general questions rather than targeted design solutions.  This study presents a novel visual inquiry generation model that can be guided to produce questions that yield the desired design solutions.  This model is trained to generate questions based on the relationships between the desired design outcome and design process, enabling it to produce such targeted questions.  To evaluate its effectiveness, we created a new dataset of 1,200 questions related to design hand sketching tasks and compared it to existing datasets that are not suited for this task.  Our model significantly outperforms existing visual inquiry generation systems and even human experts in generating questions that yield the desired design solutions, as evidenced by a 30% improvement in predicting design outcomes from questions and 10% improvement in identifying design solutions from questions in blind studies.

We examine the hypothesis that supernova explosions within galaxy clusters cause a core-to-cusp transition in their dark matter distributions. We specifically analyze how the supernova-powered gas kicks from the central most active clusters, such as M87 and Virgo, could have driven this change. We consider the scenario in which the most energetic supernovae occur within a small, densely packed region at the cluster's core and assume that the supernova-powered outburst is contained within a confined area. We also assume that the most energetic supernovives occur within a specified time frame, such as 1 billion years, and that the supernova-powered outburst is released at a constant rate. We find that, in the case of M87, the required supernova energy is roughly 10^57 ergs, and in the case of Virgo, the required energy is roughly 10^56 ergs, over the specified time frame. We also discover that, in both scenarios, the supernova-powered outburst is insufficient to cause a core-to-cusp transition. We then consider the possibility that the most energetic supernovae are dispersed throughout the cluster, and, in this scenario, the required supernova energy is significantly reduced, to around 10^54 ergs. We also find that, in this scenario, the supernova-powered outburst is capable of causing a core-to-cusp transition.

This research introduces an innovative approach for order elimination, building on existing Superior-Order Elimination techniques. Unlike prior methods, this new method employs Boolean satisfiability techniques to enhance the order reduction process. We've integrated our approach into a publicly available tool called SOE and showcased its effectiveness using diverse examples, including those from resolution calculus, which highlights the need for precise algorithms in this domain.

In this study, we investigate the properties of replicator equations for non-linear affine games with $N$ strategies in a $b$-dimensional space. We focus on mappings that maintain similarity, producing $M$ distinct Nash equilibria and corresponding replicator equations with $F_m$ functions. We identify the conditions under which these replicator equations exhibit steady states and solve the problem of finding Nash equilibria for non-linear affine games with $N$ strategies in a $b$=2-dimensional space, yielding a total of 6 distinct types of games. We also show that these replicator equations are historically determined, producing a finite tree structure under random initial conditions and with a depth of $N$ layers.

We examine the performance of a tree-based, pointwise estimator for a multivariate response regression problem, where multiple outcomes are predicted simultaneously. The estimator, applied to each individual observation, is then aggregated to form the final, global estimate. The multivariate approach is advantageous, particularly when predicting color images, by allowing the algorithm to share information across pixels. We derive conditions under which the estimator's performance at a single pixel is unaffected by other pixels, and we derive the asymptotic distribution of the global estimate. The findings indicate that the aggregated, multivariate estimator is asymptotically normal and achieves the maximum, theoretical reduction in variance. The results are validated through a simulation study and an application on color image compression.

This research focuses on the optimization of single-phase electric vehicle charging within unbalanced power distribution networks, taking into account both vehicle-side and grid-side charging constraints in a probabilistic framework. A new, decentralized charging control method is developed, which uses local power factor correction and minimizes voltage fluctuations while allowing for maximum consumer-admissible voltage non-synchrony. The algorithm is based on the optimization-restricted-ADMM framework, which iteratively solves the joint consumer-grid optimization problem and yields optimal voltage-neutralized single-phase charging profiles.

Using the density functional theory within the plane wave formalism, we have investigated the structural, elastic, and electronic properties of $SmFeO_3$ in its orthorhombic Pnma phase. Our calculations, conducted with the B3LYP functional, predicted a stable orthorhombic Pnma structure, aligning with experimental findings. The Pnma structure was found to possess lower stability compared to the orthorhombic Pbmm class, but it remains thermodynamically stable. We have also determined the single crystal elastic constants for the orthorhombic Pnma and Pbmm classes, revealing that the Pnma structure exhibits brittle behavior. Furthermore, our calculations indicate that the electronic structure of $SmFeO_3$ exhibits a direct band gap, consistent with experimental observations.

A bacterial cell's survival hinges on a delicate balance between rapid division and mitigation of DNA replication errors, a concept that can be visually represented through a topological analysis of their genome. By examining the flow of a genome's genetic material, it becomes apparent that there are distinct strategies employed by different species to navigate the delicate equilibrium between replication and error correction, and this variation can be categorized into distinct modes of existence.

The integration of data-driven technologies and data-informed approaches has become a crucial component of smart and energy-efficient buildings. These systems can be developed using data obtained from building management systems or in-field data acquisition, allowing for the creation of predictive models that optimize building operations. This study focuses on designing and validating data-informed models for building ventilation systems, which are a critical component of indoor air quality management. A data-driven approach is proposed to create an intelligent building ventilation control system, using a subset of data from building management systems to train a predictive model that automates control decisions. A data filtering and selection technique is presented to identify the most effective data for model training. A case study is conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed data-informed model against conventional control strategies and traditional data-driven models. The results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in achieving energy efficiency and maintaining optimal indoor air quality levels within the building.

We have thoroughly examined the supernova (SN) 2017gci, a unique type of superluminous SN-I, using a combination of photometric and spectroscopic data. Our analysis suggests that SN 2017gci exhibits characteristics of both hydrogen-rich and hydrogen-poor SNe-I, with the latter being more pronounced. A comparison with other SNe-I suggests that SN 2017gci may have originated from the explosion of a binary system, where a less massive star accretes material from a more massive companion. This scenario is similar to that of other SNe-I, such as SN 2015czf, with the possibility that the binary system is initially separated by a significant distance.

The well-established Stoner-Wohlfarth model has been expanded to analyze the behavior of two-dimensional materials under magnetic fields. By considering the geometric constraints of two-dimensionality, the model has been developed to predict how these materials respond to magnetic fields. A new formula has been derived to describe the critical field at which the magnetic material's magnetization switches, taking into account its shape and properties. By applying this formula, the model has been used to study how two-dimensional materials respond to in-plane magnetic fields. By comparing its predictions with existing experimental results, the model has been shown to be effective in explaining how two-dimensional materials behave. A new method has also been proposed for determining the magnetic properties of two-dimensional materials, using a combination of Stoner-Wohlfarth theory and classical mechanics.

To generate accurate dependencies, it's crucial to grasp the essence and visual aspects of each sentence and its constituent parts. However, existing neural approaches to dependency parsing overlook these elements. This paper suggests that visual understanding is a vital component in identifying dependencies and proposes Visual DepTrees, a model that considers both the visual and linguistic features of a sentence. By fusing visual and linguistic inputs, Visual DepTrees can effectively extract and process various visual cues embedded within a sentence. Moreover, to improve the model's learning process, we introduce Visual DepTree Transformer, which harmonizes language and visual inputs by employing self-attention mechanisms. Our experiments demonstrate that Visual DepTrees and Visual DepTree Transformer yield superior results compared to current state-of-the-art models on English and Chinese dependency parsing tasks.

Most machine learning models are inherently transparent, as they can display their decision-making processes through feature importance. Yet, despite their clarity, these models can be misleading due to the nature of deep convolutional networks. To address this, feature attribution techniques analyze models and provide insights into their decision-making processes. Our study assesses the effectiveness of five feature attribution techniques across various image-related tasks, including image classification, object localization, and semantic segmentation. Our results show that no single technique excels across all tasks and models. Instead, we recommend using feature attribution techniques as an initial model assessment and selecting the most suitable method for the specific requirements of the application.

We're investigating wormholes that don't preserve symmetry under reflection, specifically those with two distinct shadow patterns visible in their images. Initially, we're focusing on a specific group of wormholes consisting of two segments with different radii connected by a surface with zero thickness known as a thin shell. Researchers have previously discovered that these wormholes can display dual shadow patterns under linearized conditions, with one set appearing at low spin rates and the other at higher spin rates. Now, we're exploring the stability of these wormholes under linearization in more detail, particularly in regards to how their dual shadow patterns emerge at low spin rates. Our findings show that the dual shadow patterns appear at spin rates that increase in proportion to the wormhole's mass and the square root of the surface tension. We've also derived an equation to describe the stability of these wormholes, which reveals that higher dual shadow patterns appear at higher spin rates, an outcome that differs from the linearization stability of spherically symmetric black holes.

Given a sequence of independent random variables $\{X_i\}_{i=1}^n$, we introduce the concept of "random strides" permutation $\pi_s$ defined by a sequence of increasing integers $1<s_1<s_2<\cdots <s_n < n+1$, where each $s_i$ has a random length $l_i$, and $\pi_s$ is the permutation that rearranges $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ based on these strides. We study the entropy of this permutation $\pi_s$ for a broad class of probability measures, which includes both independent and dependent variables. We also examine the long-term behavior of the entropy of "full permutations" $\pi$ when the sequence $\{\epsilon_i\}$ is composed of independent and identically distributed variables. Our findings generalize and extend previous work of Babai-Lavault and Janvreseski-Bollob's on permutations generated by random words, as well as the work of Gao-Gao on permutations of random vectors, by broadening the applicability of these results to a wider range of probability distributions.

Trimers in the form of $H_2$ molecules are being considered as a potential component to be integrated into superconducting materials.  Theoretical studies have been conducted to examine the impact of these trimers on superconducting properties, yielding promising results.  However, further investigation through experiments is required to validate the theoretical findings.  This review aims to summarize the current state of research on trimers in superconducting materials, highlighting the key aspects to be explored and monitored in further studies.

This paper introduces a novel learning strategy, aimed at enhancing cross-domain binary classification tasks. The proposed approach leverages two types of classifiers: those that recognize instances from the source domain, as well as their reciprocal counterparts, which identify instances from the target domain. The goal is to develop a single, universal classifier that can effectively adapt to any new, unseen source domain, without requiring additional training. The method's effectiveness is supported by positive user feedback.

This paper introduces a novel approach to accurately identify the position of automobiles in images and recreate their 3D forms from pairs of images, utilizing prior knowledge specific to various automobile subcategories. The proposed method involves creating a database of known automobile models and their 3D shapes, then generating a range of possible shapes for each subcategory using a technique called non-rigid registration. The accuracy of the 3D models is then enhanced through a learning process that utilizes the differences between similar and dissimilar images, along with the knowledge of the automobile's body structure. The proposed method demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy when compared to existing techniques.

We've developed an innovative method for formulating complex queries on vast knowledge graphs, which serve as the foundation for advanced question answering systems. By mirroring the human thought process, our approach treats query generation as a generative process that combines and modifies existing queries, based on sample examples. To achieve this, we create a vast library of pre-formulated queries, which are represented as interconnected graphs, which can be easily expanded and refined. We utilize a two-stage training process where a deep generative model learns to create new queries, by either expanding or filling in pre-existing ones, and a reinforcement learning algorithm refines this model to prioritize sketches that are relevant to the given inquiry. Our proposed approach demonstrates superior performance on complex question answering tasks, outperforming both traditional and cutting-edge baselines.

This research paper focuses on developing a theoretical framework for polynomial compositions and monoid realms, which are distinct mathematical entities. It delves into analyzing these structures, exploring their relationships within the realm of multivariate polynomials and their potential applications. Specifically, the concept of polynomial compositions gives rise to a novel form of algebraic structures, including polynomial monoids and polynomial semigroups. This study demonstrates that the composition operator can be extended to various types of algebraic structures, including groups, semigroups, and commutative rings. Furthermore, the framework of monoid realms enables the creation of novel algebraic structures, including those mentioned above, as well as differential and Lie monoids. This theoretical foundation has far-reaching implications, particularly in the context of multivariate polynomial functions.

The emergence of new data sources such as mobile devices and Internet of Things has led to the development of graph databases that represent real-world systems as interconnected entities. As these systems continuously evolve, their representations in graph databases are updated in real-time to reflect the changing structure. However, current graph databases are not equipped to handle the constant influx of new data, which results in incomplete or inaccurate updates. To address this issue, we investigate the feasibility of using named entity resolution (NER) to enhance the robustness of graph databases and their ability to handle streaming data. We examine various NER methods and evaluate their performance on a range of real-world datasets, considering both their accuracy and efficiency in processing large volumes of data. The experimental results show that although NER methods can significantly improve the quality of graph databases, their efficiency varies significantly depending on the specific approach and dataset being used.

In the context of the MSSM, our research investigates the adjustments needed for various electroweak observables, particularly those influenced by oblique parameters, which serve as indicators of new physics in the electroweak sector. Our study involves a comprehensive analysis of one-loop effects contributing to these oblique adjustments, with a focus on gauge-Higgs interactions within a framework of the minimal supersymmetric standard model. By applying a combination of geometric and spectral decomposition methods, we obtain a detailed representation of the one-loop corrections to the gauge-Higgs interactions, considering both the full and simplified scenarios. Our analysis includes a thorough evaluation of the radiative corrections' behavior, taking into account the influence of non-minimal Higgs sectors. Additionally, we have developed a set of numerical tools to facilitate the comprehensive one-loop adjustments for oblique adjustments.

We introduce a novel approach to generate 3D ego-motion from dynamic single-image captures. Our method, referred to as DynPers, produces a dynamic perspective sequence along with corresponding frame-to-frame disparity and occlusion maps. To achieve this, DynPers employs a convolutional neural network that aggregates static, moving object, and background information from multiple frames into 2D feature maps, which are subsequently fed into a 3D CNN to predict all necessary outputs. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of DynPers in producing high-quality perspective views, in-frame differences, and disparity maps on both static and dynamic video benchmarks, while also outperforming existing methods in qualitative and quantitative dynamic perspective generation. Additionally, we showcase the method's capability to generate 3D animations from single-image footage.

We examine the behavior of rough differential equations with a particular emphasis on solutions interacting with a viscous medium, where the viscosity acts as a damping mechanism. By considering a one-dimensional position process $X_t$ influenced by a rough path $v$, our system includes an additional non-linear attenuation term $c(X_t)$ that depends on $X_t$. We investigate the behavior of $X_t$ under the assumption that its initial position is zero and the viscosity is negligible, which is represented by $c(0)=0$. We derive a condition on $c$ that ensures the existence of a unique solution $X_t$ for the rough differential equation. By leveraging recent advancements in controlled path probabilities, we are able to obtain precise estimates of the $p$-th moment of $X_t$ for $1 < p < 3$.

A common stochastic model representing random grains in a three-dimensional space uses independent random variables to describe the grains' lengths, leading to the application of scaling bounds in measuring the probability of a set of random grain polyhedra in a random environment. Specifically, when analyzing the probability of random polyhedra in a Burgers' equation, which models turbulence, the scaling bounds are utilized to derive upper and lower limits on the probability's behavior as the number of random grain polyhedra increases.

The integration of intelligent surfaces is seen as a pivotal technology for 6G wireless communications. This paper delves into the capabilities and applications of reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in 6G networks, concentrating on the utilization of these surfaces for dynamic beamforming in ultra-dense networks. An innovative approach is proposed, which enables intelligent surfaces to create dynamic beam patterns that adapt to the dynamic environment. Additionally, this paper examines the design challenges of these surfaces and presents potential solutions. It also discusses the feasibility of implementing these surfaces in 6G networks and offers guidance on future research directions for industry practitioners.

This paper introduces a method to simplify multi-agent probabilistic systems, specifically when they exhibit complex behaviors due to multiple equilibrium states, using a technique called stochastic switching. This method can handle systems with unpredictable events that trigger changes in behavior, and it preserves the original system's properties related to probability, without altering its essential nature. Although this technique is applicable to a broad range of stochastic multi-agent systems, its effectiveness is most notable in systems with nonlinear dynamics, and it may extend to linear systems as a particular case.

Deep learning models have shown promise in image processing tasks, particularly after being optimized for low-bitwidth. However, the current optimization techniques have a significant drawback as they require retraining the model from the beginning, which results in a substantial increase in training time as the depth of the network increases. This paper presents a novel training method that accelerates the optimization of low-bitwidth CNNs by reducing training iterations. The proposed approach, referred to as Cyclic Training with Multiple Quantization Phases (CTMQ), involves cyclic education of multiple quantization-phased CNNs within a single training session. As a result, the training time is significantly minimized, and the accuracy of low-bitwidth CNNs is simultaneously improved. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the CTMQ approach, which leads to a substantial accuracy improvement of 0.8%, 1.2%, and 2.2% for 4-bit, 2-bit, and 2-bit CNNs, respectively, in comparison to the state-of-the-art approaches.

The core-degenerate (CD) pathway for type Ia supernovae involves the merger of two white dwarfs, where the low-mass component serves as a donor, transferring mass to a more massive secondary. This process can result in a supernova explosion, which is distinct from the more commonly discussed white dwarf merger scenario. A key prediction of the CD pathway is the existence of supernovae with low iron, low mass, and low velocity velocities, as well as minimal interaction with their surroundings. Our analysis of the merger of a 0.855 and 0.125 solar mass white dwarf pair provides new insights into this pathway, including the first observation of a CD supernova progenitor. This binary system is consistent with the observed properties of the type Ia supernovae ASASSN-15ox and iPTF14hls, which exhibit low iron and mass velocities, and low velocities. Our findings suggest that the CD pathway accounts for at least some type Ia supernovae, and may be the primary mechanism for at least a subset of these events.

In large-scale educational settings, traditional teaching methods often fall short due to their inability to efficiently handle the diverse needs and backgrounds of students, which can lead to knowledge gaps that hinder student understanding and teacher effectiveness. Furthermore, students may not always be receptive to learning at the time expected. To address these challenges, this research focuses on developing educational systems capable of adapting to the unique circumstances of individual students and their ability to learn. Specifically, this work explores the concept of "anytime education" in large-scale educational environments, where educational content is tailored to the interests and abilities of each student, taking into account their preferences, current knowledge levels, and personal circumstances. The goal is to provide an anytime education framework that enables efficient learning, adapts to the evolving needs of students, and optimizes learning resources.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused unprecedented disruption and health consequences, resulting in over 4 million deaths and a global economic loss of nearly $22 trillion. While vaccines have been developed, the pace of distribution has been hindered by inefficient planning and delivery systems. A key challenge has been managing vaccine distribution and tracking storage, which varies by location, or developing digital solutions that cater to diverse requirements. To address these issues, we propose an open-source blockchain platform for immunization, which streamlines registration, reporting, and inquiry processes, making them faster, cheaper, and more reliable. This platform supports local immunization efforts, enabling participating entities to create customized solutions within their jurisdictions.

Recent advancements in NLP have enabled the development of innovative tools to support the creation of new courses. By analyzing the differences in language usage and preferences within and between courses, educators can tailor their words and message delivery to better fit specific audiences. This study investigates whether courses can be grouped into distinct categories through the analysis of linguistic patterns and preferences. Using a cutting-edge language model, we examined the textual data from course descriptions and verified our findings with an extensive corpus of student feedback and ratings. The results demonstrate that courses can be meaningfully grouped together by capturing their characteristic tone, which can inform the creation and delivery of content tailored to particular courses and student populations.

The Lattice Lippmann-Meszaros-Schwingel formalism has been used to study how the interaction potential affects the bound state energy of two complex particles. This new understanding of interaction's impact extends beyond the typical Vpen approximation, providing a loop expansion-based analysis. The resulting bound state energy is expressed as an infinite series of terms, with each term representing an interaction loop. The terms in this series can be interpreted as corrections to the Vpen approximation, and include a quantum correction that resembles quantum mechanics' 'quantum fluorescence' phenomenon. The loop expansion also reveals that particle-antiparticle symmetry breaking leads to a non-zero loop term, causing an asymmetrical shift in bound state energy.

A theoretical model is developed to investigate the decay of spin-rotation modes within a highly magnetized electron gas, with a focus on its interaction with nuclear spin and the resulting emergence of a collective spin-rotation mode. The interaction between the electron spin and the nuclear spin causes the electron's dynamics to be influenced, ultimately leading to the slow decay of the spin-rotation mode. The rate of this decay is directly proportional to the number of electrons per unit area, with a decay time that is inversely related to the square of the electron spin relaxation time and the number of electrons per unit area.

We explore the Floquet behavior of a driven quantum Rabi model in a one-dimensional circuit, using a continuous driving scheme. Our study focuses on how various parameters, including the Josephson coupling, frequency, amplitude, and detuning, affect the system's dynamics. We find that the circuit's layout and parameter settings can be tailored to exhibit conformal Floquet behavior, resulting in a variety of interesting phenomena, such as the emergence of conformal field theories and the presence of anomalous states. Furthermore, we examine the impact of high-frequency driving on the system's dynamics and investigate the possibility of harnessing non-equilibrium steady states for quantum information processing.

A significant unresolved challenge in the field of bio-signal processing involves fusing data from multiple sensors within a single algorithm. We propose a novel approach, involving a shared latent representation, to integrate and process the data from diverse sensors. This method is illustrated through a fusion algorithm designed for combining EEG and near infrared spectroscopy signals in the context of brain-computer interface applications, notably in motor task detection. The proposed algorithm is subjected to extensive experiments on three standard datasets, including two commonly used ones and an in-house experimental dataset. The results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance in motor task classification, with notable improvements in comparison to the baseline single-modal and traditional fusion methods.

The LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider has achieved significant milestones in the study of CP violation in the quark sector. This was made possible through a non-trivial mixing of the six possible quark states, which led to the observation of a substantial phase shift in the K-mesons' properties. This phenomenon, known as direct CP violation in the phi_s difference, is a key area of interest. Additionally, researchers have explored the phenomenon of matter-antimatter difference in K-meson masses, quantified as a delta-gamma-sigma difference in the K-meson mixing parameters.

This paper investigates the application of graph filters to achieve ideal control in linear network systems with graph symmetry. By using linear network systems as plant models, it is demonstrated that graph filters can effectively generate optimal control inputs for distributed control of network systems with graph symmetry. Moreover, it is shown that an infinite impulse response graph filter can be utilized to achieve ideal control if the plant model is stable, while a causal finite impulse response graph filter can be used if the plant model has a finite input-output memory. This approach is illustrated with numerical examples.

This study introduces a novel multi-sensor tracking method based on a combined adaptive birth sampler (CBAS) that tracks labeled random finite sets. The CBAS approach captures the dynamic relationship between birth rates and measurement time, deriving a unique expression for each sensor. The study presents a combined measurement model that combines all available sensors, developed using a previous analysis. The proposed method is then applied to estimate the labeled random finite set by iteratively solving two related Poisson equations. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulations, which show a significant reduction in computational complexity compared to existing methods, from cubic to quadratic order.

This study presents our collaborative findings in the 2020 edition of the
Stylized Typology Initiative's shared task on forecasting 25 key linguistic
attributes. The task involved predicting 41 languages using a combination of
univariate time series data and a novel approach based on the Long Short-Term
Memory (LSTM) architecture. The task served as a benchmark to evaluate the
effectiveness of our proposed forecasting method against existing models in
forecasting linguistic change over time. The results demonstrate that our LSTM-based
approach outperforms other models in terms of accuracy for a majority of the
languages evaluated.

The field of reinforcement learning has gained significant traction over the years, with numerous applications in areas like robotics, video games, and recommendation systems.  Despite the progress made, there are still several key challenges that need to be addressed.  One such challenge is off-policy evaluation, a problem that has garnered a lot of attention in the field.  In this problem setting, we don't have the luxury of evaluating policies using online data; instead, we rely on a fixed dataset to assess their performance.  Given its importance, off-policy evaluation has been a major focus area in the field of reinforcement learning.  In this comprehensive survey, we delve into the world of off-policy evaluation, exploring its various aspects and nuances.  We start by introducing the problem and discussing some of the fundamental assumptions that underlie some of the existing methods.  We then delve into some of the popular off-policy evaluation algorithms, examining their strengths and limitations.  We also examine some of the recent advances in the field, including methods that don't rely on any assumptions about the data-generating process.  We conclude by identifying some of the existing gaps in the field and speculating on the direction the research in off-policy evaluation might head in the future.

The Biological Warfare Threats (BMT) collection, established in 2015, aims to gather data on microorganisms of potential use in biological warfare, thereby advancing research in the field. We have discovered that the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) employs a systematic approach in selecting organisms for the collection. The Stochastic Logic Model (SLM), a probabilistic framework, was developed to mimic NAS's decision-making process, using historical data and logical rules. In our research, we refined the SLM to better represent actual collection choices and employed machine learning techniques to create a predictive model. This model was then trained on a large dataset of organisms and used to forecast future collections. Our results confirm the effectiveness of the SLM in simulating actual collection choices and suggest that it may be utilized to forecast future collections. Moreover, our model demonstrates the potential for generating accurate predictions using limited historical data and few variables. The models developed in this study can be employed by various stakeholders to forecast future collections.

The energy-momentum relationship of a strongly coupled polaron is essential for understanding its behavior, and establishing an optimal parabolic upper limit for this relationship is crucial. This study demonstrates that a parabolic upper limit exists, is continuous, and can be expressed as a specific function, and further proves that this function can be well-approximated by another function under certain conditions. By using these results, we are able to approximate the optimal parabolic upper limit for the energy-momentum relationship of a strongly coupled polaron, and our findings show that these approximations are accurate and can be verified numerically.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of operators in a holographic magnetohydrodynamic model, particularly focusing on their collapse due to super-radiant effects. The analysis reveals that the boundary operators' susceptibility to these effects is influenced by the electromagnetic interface conditions, becoming less pronounced as one deviates from the electromagnetic free-space conditions, e.g., when one replaces the electric displacement field with a generic function in the bulk. Furthermore, adjusting the electromagnetic interface conditions allows for a partial mitigation of the super-radiant effect, thereby extending the lifetime of operators on the boundary.

Our analysis delves into the relationship between two fundamental principles in quantum theory: complementarity and the property of being non-local. We examine a specific instance of complementarity arising from the contextuality debate. By considering a variant of the Schrödinger cat thought experiment, we investigate how non-locality and complementarity are intertwined in quantum queries to a joint quantum system, which in this case is the feline offspring of two quantum cats.

The cyclic decomposition theorem for the n-gon is extended to cover the case of general Riemann surfaces by applying Horowitz's concept of nonexpansive curves to develop a cyclic decomposition theorem for the universal cover.

A novel method for determining the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between metric graphs is presented, leveraging discrete Borsuk quantities to inform a strategy for graph refinement and equivalence through embedding.

This article presents improved calculations for the resolvents of homogenized fourth-order differential operators with periodically repeating coefficients. These more comprehensive estimates serve as crucial components in the proof of energy decay for a long-term system, which is influenced by a high-order, time-invariant differential equation with periodically repeating coefficients of quadratic order. Although the underlying system may have limited dissipation, its behavior can be accurately modeled by its homogenized counterpart.

Recent advancements in English task-driven dialogue frameworks have been highly
successful, but their effectiveness in non-English languages remains unknown due to
a lack of research. This study investigates the performance of a comprehensive
multilingual framework across 11 languages by analyzing the significance of
conversation history in task completion. The investigation compares the framework's
performance with a basic version without conversation history and a more advanced
approach using a single previous response. The results demonstrate a consistent
increase in performance as more conversation history is considered, but also
reveal that a simple single previous response model achieves comparable results to
the more complex frameworks. These findings provide crucial insights for the
development of task-driven dialogue frameworks for non-English languages.

This abstract provides an overview of Smt-Switch, a C++ interface designed to work with any SMT solver in a uniform manner. Originally created to facilitate experimentation and testing, the interface offers a highly abstract approach to interacting with SMT solving. This abstraction enables users to focus on the solving task without being restricted by the limitations of individual solver libraries. A key feature of Smt-Switch is its ability to function with any SMT solver, without requiring modifications or source code changes.

A novel, distinct approach to determining the spectral distribution within a specific framework of quasi-exactly solvable systems is proposed. This approach involves calculating the higher-order statistical moments of the spectral density, thereby providing essential information about the underlying quantum mechanics problem. By utilizing this method, the quasi-exactly solvable nature of a specific system is confirmed, and the exact eigenvalues are determined for a particular parameter range. Furthermore, the results of this method are compared with those obtained from the generalized Bender-Dunne polynomial and the spectral density of another quasi-exactly solvable system.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to improved performance in various computer vision tasks through larger and more complex models. However, this performance gain typically comes with a substantial increase in the number of parameters, operations, and memory requirements, which can be a significant barrier for deployment on devices with limited resources. This paper presents a novel technique for designing more efficient CNN models that leverage fewer parameters and FLOPS while maintaining competitive performance. The key innovation involves modifying the convolutional kernel to incorporate redundant information, enabling a more accurate classification outcome without adding additional complexity. The proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing models and has been successfully applied to the Shufflenet and MobileNet architectures, yielding enhanced performance in image classification and retrieval tasks.

The DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission aims to collide with Dimorphos, a secondary asteroid accompanying Didymos, causing a change in Dimorphos' rotation period and speed, potentially altering its orbital velocity. This impact may create boulders that move between the primary and secondary asteroids, affecting their relative motion. To study this phenomenon, researchers simulated multiple impacts and granular dynamics on both asteroids, using a 3D discrete element method. The analysis revealed that boulders can travel up to 100 meters in a short time frame, and the rotation of each asteroid influences the boulders' trajectories. This interaction can cause a delay in the boulders' arrival on the secondary asteroid, potentially altering the velocity and trajectory of the boulders impacting Dimorphos. The results also indicate that boulders ejected from the impact on Dimorphos can travel to Didymos, and the likelihood of this happening is higher if the impact occurs on the secondary asteroid's equator or near its equatorial region.

Our research involves examining static, charged, spherically symmetric scalar field configurations in the vicinity of a Reissner-Nordstrom black hole. We found that the general scalar field patterns are represented by a specific equation and that the scalar field and its associated energy-momentum tensor exhibit a complex, self-similar pattern. We were able to establish a set of fundamental equations that govern the behavior of these self-similar patterns. We then analyzed the thermodynamic properties of these self-similar scalar field configurations and found that the black hole's mass, spatial radius, and charge are all interconnected. We also discovered that the mass of these complex field configurations is directly proportional to their spatial radius and charge, and that the thermodynamic properties of these complex field configurations follow a set of rules that are similar to those of a black hole. We then used these findings to test a hypothesis that the complex field patterns do not contradict a set of rules known as no-hair theorems.

The recent observation of active-sterile neutrino oscillations at the KATRIN experiment has provided valuable insights into the sterile neutrino framework. Nevertheless, the mixing between active and sterile neutrinos poses a significant non-linear issue that affects the experiment's ability to measure the electron anti-neutrino mass. To investigate this challenge, the sterile neutrino mixing with the active neutrino sector is re-examined under the assumption of non-linearity. Our analysis reveals that the sterile neutrino mass must be below the 2 GeV range to prevent the sterile neutrino from being undetectable by the KATRIN experiment. This finding has significant implications for theories involving sterile neutrinos at GeV scales, including active-sterile mixing and the origin of neutrino oscillation phenomena.

The majority of recent self-supervised denoising methods utilize the concept of duality to separate clean and noisy images. However, due to the inherent complexity of these images, the separation process is often hindered by the presence of artifacts. Consequently, these artifacts can negatively impact the performance of subsequent denoising networks. To address this issue, we introduce CVF-SID, a novel self-supervised denoising method that relies on a cyclic, multi-variate function to break down the disturbance from images. The proposed approach is composed of two key components: a univariate, multi-scale filter and a cross-correlation function. The filter is designed to capture the low-frequency, smooth aspects of images. The cross-correlation function, on the other hand, is used to measure the similarity between clean and noisy images. By combining these components, CVF-SID effectively eliminates artifacts and improves the performance of subsequent denoising networks. Experiments conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CVF-SID in enhancing the performance of various denoising methods.

The goal of sparse reconstruction involves uncovering a signal of low-regularity from a limited set of measurements, and it has been found that a sufficient amount of measurements are required to capture the essential information. Previous studies established that $\mu$-sensitivities are proportional to the signal's sparsity, and certain results have been obtained for specific signals. This paper sets a minimum limit on the number of measurements needed to fully reconstruct a signal of sparsity $k$ by exploiting the knowledge of $\mu$, and these results are also applicable to a broader class of signals. This new understanding is based on the following key findings: (1) a sufficient condition for a signal's reconstructability in terms of $\mu$ and the number of measurements, and (2) a lower bound on the number of measurements required to fully capture the essential information.

Formulating agreement indices for multiple random variables can be complicated, 
especially for more than two variables at a time. Although overlapping 
correlations can be measured through various indices, such as the multiple 
Pearson correlation coefficient, a widely applicable and efficient 
generalization for multiple variables does not exist. In this work, we introduce 
a novel, symmetric, and non-linear index for agreement that can be calculated 
for an arbitrary number of random variables, including scalar ones. This new 
measure extends the union and intersection agreements in the context of two 
random variables and is based on a recently introduced parameter for 
categorical variables, which allows for a deeper analysis of data structures.

Deep reinforcement learning methods have gained popularity for automating robot learning due to their ability to provide direct rewards without the need for detailed modeling.  However, the efficiency of DRLL still raises questions about its suitability for complex tasks.  This research aims to address these concerns on a 7-DoF robot performing a pick and place task.  First, we observed that the learning process in DRLL can be slowed by the high cost of evaluating actions in the physical world.  Next, we proposed an innovative approach to reduce this 'end-effect cost' by creating a zero-cost evaluation system.  Specifically, we developed an 'end-effect drive' mechanism that uses a flexible simulation environment to optimize motor control, allowing for faster and more efficient learning.  Our results show that the proposed method not only accelerates the learning process but also improves the robot's performance in the long run.  This breakthrough has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of DRLL and pave the way for its practical application in robotics.

A fundamental equation linking the renormalized rate constant of a reaction involving two particles in a distorted harmonic potential and the system's thermal energy has been established. The rate constant formula incorporates corrections that arise from higher-order potential terms, which depend on frequency. By comparing the thermal energy with the rate constant in a system at absolute zero, a scaling factor is introduced. This scaling factor, which is dependent on higher-order potential terms, can be used to predict the type of distortion present in the potential. The study also shows that in systems with certain types of distortion, the thermal energy will follow a simple harmonic relationship with temperature.

We have performed a detailed analysis of the two-point correlation function in two-dimensional conformal field theories within the context of Liouville CFTs crossed with generic crosscap boundaries. Our analysis has revealed that the leading and subleading contributions to this correlation function arise from a specific class of bulk and boundary operators known as the "first type", which are defined as $\mathcal{V}_0$. Notably, the inclusion of crosscap boundaries does not introduce any new information beyond what is already present in the one-point function, but rather leads to a straightforward product relationship that facilitates the computation of the two-point correlation function. Our results are applicable to both the Belavin-Klimov and the Zamolodchikov two-point functions.

In the aftermath of the 2020 U.S. presidential election, numerous researchers conducted studies on the impact of false social media information. One such study focused on how Twitter suspended accounts claiming affiliation with President Donald Trump, an action taken as part of an effort to combat misinformation. The study examined elements associated with suspended accounts, categorizing them into three groups: those related to the 2020 U.S. presidential election, general news, or sports. The study found that suspended accounts in the election category often included local election officials and officials' personal accounts, which may have provided fact-based information. In contrast, accounts in the news pool from this category were largely associated with pro-Trump media outlets and other non-mainstream sources. The study also found that suspended accounts in the sports category were largely automated accounts that spread fake information. The study's findings have implications for identifying and preventing the spread of misinformation on social media.

This study aims to evaluate the feasibility of detecting graviton production at the LHC through electron-hadron collisions. As the LHC upgrade approaches, it's essential to investigate whether the existing detectors can handle the increased luminosity and design new instruments accordingly. Given that the LHC already detects proton-proton and proton-lead collisions, a thorough analysis of electron-hedron collisions is necessary to assess its potential contribution. The study involves a simulation of electron beam production from a plasma source utilizing the LHC's existing proton synchrotron as a comparison point. The simulation data indicates that a 1 GeV electron beam can be produced in 2.5 ns with a frequency of 10 Hz and an energy of 1 GeV, meeting the LHC's time and frequency standards. The study also found that a 1 GeV electron beam can be captured by the LHC's magnets and that a new electron source can operate at a time frame of 2.5 ns. The study concludes that a future electron source at the LHC can produce 10^10 GeV-electrons per second. The study also discusses the potential for detecting the production of a 10^-17 g graviton in the LHC's detector at the end of its 10-year operation period.

Crowdsourced datasets often contain errors and ambiguity, which can be particularly problematic when data is limited.  To address this issue, our research explores the use of ensemble learning to create a system capable of identifying inconsistencies within crowdsourced data.  We utilize uncertainty metrics to pinpoint user reliability, which are then utilized to eliminate or mitigate the effects of inaccurate or ambiguous crowd-sourced data on subsequent machine learning tasks.  To this end, our approach combines the use of ensemble learning with uncertainty analysis and a new method for modeling human judgment, which we refer to as 'human softmax'.  By applying this approach, we are able to create a more robust and reliable dataset that can be utilized for machine learning tasks.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we present a case study of a crowdsourced dataset used for classifying 2D images into 10 categories.  Our analysis reveals that the uncertainty metrics and uncertainty analysis developed in this study are capable of accurately predicting user reliability, which is then utilized to create a more reliable dataset.  Furthermore, our approach is also applicable to datasets collected through other forms of human interaction, such as games.

In the context of the 5G cellular network, vehicle-to-everything (V2X) applications, such as vehicle collision avoidance, traffic management, and entertainment, necessitate distributed V2X (D-V2X) services. These services, typically provided by multiple base stations working in a multi-connect state, are characterized by high mobility and dynamic connectivity requirements. However, the base stations' limited processing capabilities make it difficult to achieve these adaptive multi-connect states. A novel, environment-aware learning method is proposed to address this issue, which utilizes a deep Q-network's ability to predict base station states' performance in a given environment. The method trains a Q-network to make data-driven predictions about base station quality based on environment characteristics, and a greedy algorithm uses these predictions to determine the optimal multi-connect configuration. The proposed method significantly outperforms traditional static and mobile V2X approaches in terms of network performance.

The 10-year anniversary of ImageNet provides an ideal time to reflect on the rapid progress of machine learning, particularly deep learning, which has achieved remarkable success since 2011. A comprehensive study is conducted to examine the key developments in the field of artificial intelligence since the inception of ImageNet, tracking progress through key benchmark evaluations, notable research breakthroughs, and influential projects over the past decade. The study highlights the significant impact of the computer vision community on the development of artificial intelligence as a whole. The analysis also reveals the evolving composition of the research landscape, shifting from a decentralized, collaborative approach to a more centralized one dominated by a few prominent organizations. A set of recommendations is offered for the future research roadmap, emphasizing the importance of innovation, collaboration, and innovation to ensure continued growth and improvement in artificial intelligence research.

Feature toggles, a method of controlling new functionality in existing code, has become widely adopted in industry practices. Studies have shown its benefits, yet the impact it has on large software projects remains unclear. This research investigates how feature toggles are used in open-source software, focusing on its relationship with issues and merge conflicts within branches. Using 1,500 GitHub repositories, we found that most projects use feature toggles, with half of them utilizing them in less than 10% of their branches. The results also show a positive correlation between feature toggle use and reduced merge conflicts, as well as a link between feature toggle diversity and increased issues. Conversely, we found that feature toggle density is not correlated with the metric. A case study of 7 repositories revealed that feature toggles were primarily used for feature development, testing, and experimental code, but not for stability or security enhancements.

The concept of enstrophy is often seen as a result of the Euler equations' invariance to M\"obius transformations, a characteristic that also leads to the Benjamin--Benjamin--Lange (BBM) equation's invariance to the same mathematical property. Building on the underlying symmetry of the BBM equation, it's possible to develop a broader set of equations that retain this invariance and explore their key characteristics, including solutions and conservation laws.

This study introduces a novel neural network architecture for categorizing large datasets of 3D point clouds in conjunction with 2D text documents. The system is specifically designed to facilitate research in Assyriology, where thousands of newly digitized cuneiform tablets can be analyzed each day by Assyriological experts, who annotate each new discovery. Our objective is to develop an automated system that can process these texts to accurately categorize cuneiform tablets based on their content. By leveraging a combination of deep learning models, we create a system that can efficiently categorize large datasets of unstructured 3D point clouds in real-time, showcasing its potential applications in Assyriology.

The recent measurement of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment by the Fermilab and CERN collaborations significantly deviates from the Standard Model prediction, which has prompted numerous theoretical attempts to resolve the discrepancy. In this study, we consider a scenario where the Standard Model is supplemented by a spin-2 particle, denoted as $\rho_\mu$, that primarily contributes to the one-loop level of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment.
